web_blocks.html: Executive Thesis: Qualcomm Incorporated (NASDAQ: QCOM) remains a 31.13% ROIC semiconductor and patent-licensing franchise pivoting toward Automotive ($6.00B FY26, +51.7% YoY) and IoT ($7.13B) [23, 32]. Yet our Pass 1 audit of the audited FY2026 Form 10-K and November 2026 SEC filings uncovered major hidden frictions [28, 29, 31]. Two customers represent 42% of revenue, China represents 42% ($18.08B), foundry commitments stand at $18.6B ($13.8B due in FY27), and AWS holds a 25M-share ($1.8B) contra-revenue warrant [31]. Capital returns ran at 134.9% of FCF while 46M new shares kept ending shares flat (-0.2%), and a $4.0B bond sale raised pro forma debt to $17.10B [28, 29, 31, 32].

On Friday, November 20, 2026, shares fell -7.45% on 22.22M shares (1.58x–1.68x average volume) to close at $149.94 [24]. That drop placed QCOM into STAGE_4 (CAP_REJECTED) and breached our prior $150.07 structural stop [24]. Adjusted for flat share counts, higher interest, and warrant dilution, Base Fair Value drops to $170.00 ($164.75 probability-weighted EV, +9.9%). We assign EXIT_IMMEDIATELY on all 30.0 held shares (raising $4,498.20 -> 100% CASH) and REJECTED (TIER_0) for new capital.

web_blocks.html: Near-Term Proof Points Before Re-Underwriting: We will keep QCOM off the active shortlist until four measurable milestones turn positive. First, Q1 FY27 Data Center sales must beat $650M without pulling QCT EBT margin below guidance [32]. Second, inventory ($8.64B, 156 DIO) must turn back into cash against the $13.8B FY27 purchase obligations [31]. Third, share repurchases must actually shrink share count net of M&A and $4.1B unvested RSUs [31]. Fourth, shares must form a multi-week Stage 1 base above $144.59 and reclaim the $184.39 30-week average [24].
Note on Methodology: Chapters 1 through 6 were audited strictly price-blind in Pass 1 before reviewing live November 20 quotes, technicals, and portfolio positions in Pass 2.

book_paragraphs: Welcome to our refreshed institutional investment monograph on Qualcomm Incorporated as of the November 20, 2026 market close. If you take away one core lesson from this companion update, let it be why rigid stop discipline and balance-sheet forensics exist to protect you from story stocks in transition.

One week ago, Qualcomm traded at $172.47 above its 200-day moving average, and our prior dossier held 30 existing shares with a firm structural invalidation stop at $150.07 while waiting for support. Over the past seven days, two things changed decisively. First, our blind Pass 1 audit of the full FY2026 Form 10-K and mid-November SEC filings exposed far heavier dilution, debt, and concentration friction than headline earnings suggested. Second, on Friday, November 20, Qualcomm plunged 7.45 percent on 22.22 million shares to close at $149.94—slicing cleanly through our $150.07 structural stop into Stage 4.

Look at what the audited footnotes revealed before we ever glanced at Friday's stock price. While Qualcomm spent $7.82 billion on buybacks and $3.85 billion on dividends—134.9 percent of its $8.65 billion free cash flow—it issued 46 million new shares for the $2.62 billion Modular acquisition, the $2.27 billion Alphawave purchase, and employee stock grants, leaving ending shares essentially flat (-0.2 percent). To fund that expansion, Qualcomm borrowed $4.00 billion in 5.0 to 5.8 percent senior notes on November 12, lifting pro forma debt to $17.10 billion. Meanwhile, two customers account for 42 percent of revenue, China accounts for 42 percent, $18.6 billion in unconditional foundry obligations sit on the ledger, and Amazon holds a 25-million-share ($1.8 billion) contra-revenue warrant.

When we plugged those Pass 1 realities into Chapter 7's valuation model, our Base Fair Value moved down from $195.00 to $170.00, with a Bear Case of $115.00 and a Bull Case of $215.00. At $149.94, Qualcomm trades at 15.54 times FY2027 trough consensus earnings and 32.3 times SBC-adjusted economic free cash flow ($5.20 billion), offering just +9.9 percent probability-weighted expected return against a broken Stage 4 chart.

Our Dual Verdict is therefore unambiguous. On your existing 30 shares split evenly between Charles Schwab and Robinhood ($4,868.78 cost basis, $4,498.20 market value, -$370.58 loss), the holding action is EXIT_IMMEDIATELY: sell all 30 shares now because the $150.07 stop broke on heavy volume, and keep 100 percent of the $4,498.20 proceeds in US cash during a 10-distribution-day market Downtrend. For new capital, we assign REJECTED (Tier 0) until Qualcomm carves a durable Stage 1 base and proves clean economic cash conversion.

book_subsections.title: How to Follow This Refreshed Monograph: From Blind Footnotes to Stop Execution
paragraphs: Notice how our two-pass workflow prevented confirmation bias from creeping into this refresh. In Chapters 1 through 6, our Pass 1 audit stripped out every prior target, stop, and verdict before reading the audited FY2026 Form 10-K, the November 13 senior-notes 8-K, the November 19 Form 4 insider sale, and Arm Holdings' November 4 Form 6-K appellate disclosure. That price-blind discipline surfaced the $2.62 billion Modular deal, the -$607 million Nonreportable segment loss, the $1.8 billion AWS contra-revenue warrant, the $4.1 billion unvested RSU overhang, and the $18.6 billion foundry commitments.

In Chapters 7 through 9, we reviewed the November 20 market data and ran the numbers fresh. Instead of stretching multiples or lowering our prior $150.07 stop to rationalize holding a falling stock, we enforced the upward-only stop rule strictly. Closing at $149.94 on 1.58 times average volume triggered an immediate exit of all 30 shares, freeing $4,498.20 in cash and cutting high-beta risk in a 233.5 percent beta-weighted portfolio.

As you listen through Chapters 1 to 9, pay close attention to the four clear gates that would bring Qualcomm back onto our buy list later in 2027: Data Center proving $650 million-plus quarterly scale without gross-margin erosion, inventory turning back into cash from 156 days, net share count actually shrinking, and a confirmed weekly Stage 2 reclaim above $184.39. Until those gates pass, cash preservation is the winning trade.

Let us also note what makes this update a textbook example of continuous underwriting. Every blind spot we uncovered—from the 42 percent customer and China concentration to the $1.8 billion AWS contra-revenue warrant and the -$607 million Nonreportable segment loss—came straight from primary SEC filings before we checked Friday's stock price. When the live November 20 close simultaneously confirmed a -7.45 percent high-volume breakdown below $150.07, our fundamental caution and technical stop pointed in the exact same direction: exit all 30 shares immediately, park 100 percent of proceeds in cash, and move QCOM to Rejected (Tier 0) until both the chart and cash conversion heal.

book_subsections.title: Chapter-by-Chapter Guide to What Changed in This Refresh
paragraphs: If you read our November 13 monograph, four concrete updates reshape the investment conclusion today. First, Chapters 1, 2, 3, and 6 now incorporate the full audited FY2026 Form 10-K footnotes and mid-November filings: $6.0 billion in acquisitions including $2.62 billion for Modular Inc., 42 percent top-two customer and China concentration, $18.6 billion in foundry purchase obligations, $17.10 billion in pro forma debt following the $4.00 billion notes offering, and 134.9 percent free-cash-flow payout leaving ending shares flat at 1,072 million.

Second, Chapter 7 re-prices intrinsic value on those audited inputs, bringing our Base Case down from $195.00 to $170.00 (Bear $115.00, Bull $215.00) and showing that $149.94 still trades at 32.3 times SBC-adjusted economic free cash flow. Third, Chapter 8 documents Friday's Stage 4 breakdown below our $150.07 structural stop and reconciles the facts ledger Stage 1 tag against live TradingView averages. Fourth, Chapter 9 translates every finding into immediate execution across Charles Schwab and Robinhood, locking in a controlled -$370.58 exit and restoring dry powder.

Finally, notice how transparent risk control keeps your portfolio agile during a broad semiconductor selloff. Exiting 30 shares at $149.94 raises $4,498.20 in cash and trims high-beta exposure inside a 233.5 percent beta-weighted portfolio while preserving your capital for cleaner Stage 2 leaders once the S&P 500 exits its 10-distribution-day downtrend.
